compiled_rows: Mysterious, rock-hard blue oak forms this
small, round shield.
Made from a large armadillo's hide, this shield
is remarkably light and harder than iron.
Silver leaf gives this helmet a lovely shine.
A narrow slit lets the wearer see.
This helmet has a point like a beak. Its crest
shows a bird in flight, a sign of courage
in the face of death.
A shield of giant tortoise shell, far stronger
than anything made from ordinary ore.
This pure white dress somehow warms the heart.
Legend says the spirits guard whoever wears it.
Light, tough martial garb that breaks
an attacker's blade.
Breathable yet sturdy, this armor supposedly
keeps its wearer cool.
Kanem's warriors carried this sturdy shield.
Their kingdom flourished in 11th-century
central Africa.
A knight in the grip of a strange superstition
is said to have worn this armor. The design is
in dreadful taste.
Linked rings strengthen this armor. Legend says
it glowed red in battle when a god protected
the knight wearing it.
Practical but a little heavy, this chainmail
was worn by Timur, ruler of the Timurid Empire
that thrived in the 14th century.
Peacock feathers adorn the back of this mail.
It was made to turn heads and offers only
modest protection.
The ancient Aztec warriors of Tula are said
to have worn this legendary helmet to summon
courage in battle.
The black garb of Eastern ninja. It offers
fine protection and lets them move freely
without drawing attention.
Fine armor with a mysterious yellow sheen.
No one knows its age or materials.
A splendid vest of giant jaguar fur, said
to come from the legendary Jaguar God.
This sinister armor was found among a knight's
effects. He sold his soul to the devil
for power. It is said to choose its wearer.
This eerie gown offers excellent protection.
A tyrannical empress is said to have worn it
when she was assassinated.
The Taira commander Noritsune wore this fine
armor when he drowned at Dan-no-ura.
Attila, king of the ancient Huns and feared
throughout Europe, wore this superb armor.
An excellent, eerie shield modeled on
Medusa's hair.
Saladin, the Muslim hero who fought
the Crusaders, wore this armor. It's seen
as the mark of a just and virtuous person.
Charles Martel of the Franks wore this
superb armor at the Battle of Tours-Poitiers.
Sturdy and handsome, it's fit for a king.
This sturdy shield shines of its own accord.
It's said to belong to Minerva, goddess of war
and one of the twelve Olympians.

2866: Silver leaf gives this helmet a lovely shine. A narrow slit lets the wearer see.
Keep the silver leaf and move the complete first sentence onto its own row.
2867: This helmet has a point like a beak. Its crest shows a bird in flight, a sign of courage in the face of death.
Make the crest and its meaning clear without keeping the old catalogue fragments.
2869: This pure white dress somehow warms the heart. Legend says the spirits guard whoever wears it.
Keep both source facts in complete sentences that fit their own rows.
2872: Kanem's warriors carried this sturdy shield. Their kingdom flourished in 11th-century central Africa.
Restore the warriors and the flourishing kingdom in two direct sentences.
2876: Peacock feathers adorn the back of this mail. It was made to turn heads and offers only modest protection.
Restore the location of the feathers and the maker’s emphasis on appearance over practical use.
2877: The ancient Aztec warriors of Tula are said to have worn this legendary helmet to summon courage in battle.
Attribute the helmet’s traditional use to the warriors and keep the cultural terms intact.
2879: Fine armor with a mysterious yellow sheen. No one knows its age or materials.
Retain its protective quality and shine. Keep both unknowns without a technical catalogue construction.
2887: Charles Martel of the Franks wore this superb armor at the Battle of Tours-Poitiers. Sturdy and handsome, it's fit for a king.
Keep the beauty, strength and royal comparison. Correct the full-width F and avoid assigning Charles Martel a title.
2888: This sturdy shield shines of its own accord. It's said to belong to Minerva, goddess of war and one of the twelve Olympians.
Restore the self-generated light and Minerva’s place among the Twelve.
